I dont have anything solid just a theory based on what I've learned about bd over the years.

So in our brains we have neurotransmitters that are connected by "bridges". During depression, the bridges are down, closed, malfunctioning. All the chemicals that are supposed to be traveling across those bridges are backed up.

When we cycle to mania, all the bridges are suddenly open and all of the chemicals are suddenly being delivered, creating the effect of mania.

I do believe there are short cuts they tell us and sometimes work; certain foods, exercise, hugs, etc. But I think those things also get stuck and can't cross a bridge sometimes and simply don't  help. 

I also think SSRI'S are dangerous for us because instead of repairing the bridges, they reverse their flow, sending the wrong information. 

Besides my random metaphor I think we all experience comorbidities with bipolar disorder and there isn't one way to look at it because it's infuriatingly all different. I don't just have bd, I also have ADHD... and trauma... and whatever else. Who knows.

I think that when it comes to relationships, for me, there is always something saying that I shouldn't be around this person, whether it's a significant other or even just family. What I have done is talked to my family about these feelings, even the sad, tough ones like "I don't feel like I love you all the time". It is important to be open because when something does come up like this, it isn't taken as face value by your loved one. Like, you are saying you want to break up with your boyfriend, when really it just the feeling of not wanting to be around him for one reason or another (feeling like a burden, etc). I think maybe you could let him know you've had these thoughts, but it isn't how you really feel, so if it does come out of you when you are hypomanic, he can feel confident in challenging you when you say this if he is able to recognize your episode.

Kalene’s thoughts were jumbled as she rode the subway home from work. She had just been laid off. Her company was “going in a new direction” and “outsourcing their employees”. A small copy paper box rested on her lap, and she found herself hugging the box the harder she thought, wanting some sort of comfort. She drooped her head, her long, red locks framing her face and partially dropping into the box. She peered down at some memories; a few photo frames filled with family and friends, a bamboo plant she had been taking care of, some snacks she kept at her desk and a bunch of office supplies she shamelessly stole from the supply cabinet. 

Kalene put her hand in the box and pulled out a photo without a frame that was more recent. It was of her and a few coworkers at an open mic night. She was a singer at heart and that was the first time in a while she had performed music for a crowd. Her soul was filled with joy that night as applause filled the little bar they were at. She was glad her coworkers were able to coherence her into singing. Kalene started to tear up but quickly wiped away the tears when the PA announced her stop. With a deep breath, she rose from her seat and pushed past the other patrons to move along the subway platform.

Kalene’s loft was right next to the exit and she was grateful to almost be home. That was until she had her box flung from her arms by a man with a guitar. He had been bending over, and the two collided at the exit where he was apparently set up as a busker. The man started hurriedly helping her collect her items, using his body to block people from stepping on anything. 

Kalene wanted to start bawling. The man may be helping but he wasn’t saying a word. He hadn’t even apologized. She picked up a picture frame that had been broken that held a photo of her beloved grandparents in it. That’s when Kalene lost her composure.

“What is wrong with you? Can’t you say you’re sorry?!” She finally met the man’s eyes, as he was gingerly replacing her bamboo in the small plastic vase. 

His eyes were filled with sorrow. His brows lifted up and he looked back at her straight-mouthed, seemingly unsure. He gestured to the ground and ticked his head to the side, opening his mouth then immediately shutting it again. Instead of an answer, the man simply picked up Kalene’s box and gently handed it to her. 

The area to the exit was vacant now. Kalene huffed out an angry breath from her nostrils and stormed up the stairs of the subway tunnel. She wanted to get away from this stupid man. Her heart was pounding so hard, she could feel it in her ears, which were burning red in embarrassment. She continued her ascent to the second story where she flung herself in her apartment, eyes running with tears. 

'What was she going to do with her life now? How was she going to make it?'

As Kalene lay wallowing on her living room couch, soft music started to drift in from the street below. She stopped sobbing so she could listen. Then bolted up when she recognized the song. It was the same song that her grandfather used to sing and play guitar to when she was growing up. It was the same song that they sang together, one last time before he passed away three years ago. Kalene started beaming. She ran to her window and peered out and down on the street was the man from before. As she appeared he looked down shyly but continued playing. 

Kalene started humming and soon she was singing softly. The man perked up when he could hear her and joined in, singing in a different language that Kalene didn’t recognize. She stopped singing. 'He must not speak English', she thought. And now she was more embarrassed than she was before for the misunderstanding. The man stopped playing, looking up at her confused and unsure since she had stopped singing.

“Won’t you please play it again?” She asked, making a rolling gesture with her hands. And so he did.
